rows: View from the Window at Le Gras

This is the oldest photograph that still exists. Nicéphore Niépce set a camera in an upstairs window in France and let sunlight draw on a metal plate for hours. The roofs, a pear tree and a barn show up as blurry shapes, and the sun seems to light both sides because it moved while he waited.
Look at the buildings. Why do you think there is light on both the left and the right side?
The Original Plate

This is the real metal plate Niépce used in 1826 or 1827. Under the right light you can find roofs and a chimney in the silvery smudges. The plate is so fragile that it is kept in a sealed case, and the picture above it is a version made to be easier to see.
Can you find a straight line that might be a rooftop?
Stem of Leaves and Flowers

William Henry Fox Talbot made pictures like this before his camera pictures worked. He laid a flower on paper coated with silver chemicals and let the sun print its outline. He called them photogenic drawings, meaning drawings made by light.
Find the thin stem. Which parts of the flower look the palest?
Two Sitters in a Daguerreotype

Two people sit close together in this small daguerreotype, a picture on a mirror-polished silver plate. Each daguerreotype is one of a kind, and you have to tilt it to see the image. They were kept in little cases to protect the silver.
They had to sit very still. How long can you hold a smile without moving?
Portrait of Constance Talbot
Constance Talbot sits in profile, her head outlined in soft shadow. Her husband, William Henry Fox Talbot, made pictures of her and his home, Lacock Abbey, while he was inventing paper photography.
Which way is she looking? What might she have been thinking about while she sat so still?
The Chess Players
Two men in top hats sit at a table, playing chess. Early paper photographs needed many seconds of exposure, so everyone had to hold still, which makes a quiet game like chess a good choice.
Who do you think is winning?
Boulevard du Temple

Louis Daguerre took this picture of a busy Paris street from his window. The exposure took minutes, so moving carriages and walkers vanished. One man stood still to have his boots shined, and he became probably the first person ever photographed.
Find the man at the corner having his shoes polished. Where did all the other people go?
Three Portraits in a Case
Early photographs were small and precious, so they were kept in velvet-lined cases, like this one with three oval portraits. People carried them like tiny pictures of loved ones.
What does a keepsake of yours look like? Where do you keep it?
Abby Frances Snow, Age Two and a Half
A little girl in a ruffled dress sits for a daguerreotype. Toddlers rarely stay still, so pictures of very young children from this time are rare and special.
How do you think the photographer got a two-year-old to stay still?
Two Plant Specimens
Talbot printed real plants onto paper by laying them under glass in the sun. The pink color comes from the chemicals and from toning the paper. Each print is a perfect shadow of a living flower.
Count the flower shapes. Which one is the biggest?
Self-Portrait

Robert Cornelius, a lamp maker from Philadelphia, took this picture of himself outside his father's store. He took the lens cap off, ran into the frame and stood still for several minutes. It is often called the first photographic selfie.
He wrote on the back, "The first light picture ever taken." What would you write on the back of your selfie?
View of the Predikherenei, Ghent
Buildings were perfect for early photography because they never moved. This daguerreotype shows old houses beside a canal in Ghent, Belgium, just after the process was shared with the world.
Look at the windows. How many can you count?
Portrait of Two Men
Hill and Adamson, a painter and a chemist in Scotland, made calotype portraits with strong light and shadow. Hill arranged poses the way he would in a painting.
What do you think the two men are thinking about?
Peter S. Du Ponceau
Robert Cornelius opened one of the first photo studios in America in 1840. His sitter here, an elderly Philadelphia lawyer born in France, shows how photography started to become a business.
What do you notice about the man's face? What would you ask him?
Winter Trees Reflected in a Pond
Talbot photographed bare trees mirrored in still water. It is a calm picture made of lines and reflections, and one of the earliest photographs taken just for its beauty.
Can you find where the real trees stop and their reflections begin?
The Oldest Family Photograph in Brazil

A French priest named Louis Compte brought the daguerreotype to Rio de Janeiro in 1840. This picture of Colonel João José Carneiro de Mendonça and his family, made in 1841, is known as the oldest family photograph in Brazil.
How many people are in the family? Who might be the oldest?
A 111-Year-Old Grandmother and Her Family
A family traveling to see young Emperor Pedro II crowned in Brazil had this daguerreotype taken. The oldest woman, Maria Meis, is said to have been 111 years old.
Count the generations from the oldest person to the youngest.
Peasant Father and His Son
A father and son in simple clothes lean together for a camera. Many early photographs were of rich people, so a portrait of ordinary country folk is a treat.
What do you think the father is feeling?
Moulin de la Galette
Hippolyte Bayard went up to Montmartre, then a village of windmills on the edge of Paris, and photographed an old mill. Today the hill is covered with cafes and the white Sacré-Cœur church.
Find the windmill's sails. Which way is the wind blowing?
Chair in a Garden
Bayard, one of photography's inventors, liked quiet corners. This plain garden chair, with its shadows, is a simple picture that makes you wonder who just got up.
Who do you think was sitting here a minute ago?
Old House Being Restored
Early photographers made records of old buildings that were being repaired or torn down. Bayard photographed this house with its shutters and scaffolding in Paris.
Count the shuttered windows.
Windmills of Montmartre
Montmartre was once covered in windmills that ground grain. Bayard photographed them from a field, years before artists and cafes arrived.
How many windmills can you count?
The Colonnade of the Madeleine
The Madeleine church in Paris looks like a Greek temple. Bayard framed its columns so they march into deep shadow, using the new camera to study light and geometry.
Count the columns you can see.
Earliest Known Photograph of a Living Animal

This daguerreotype, taken in Rome by Joseph-Philibert Girault de Prangey, is believed to be the earliest photograph of a living animal. The animal rests by a cart and stayed calm long enough for the exposure.
Find the animal near the bottom of the picture. Why did it have to stay so still?
Articles of China

Talbot lined up his china on shelves and photographed it, and he suggested in his book The Pencil of Nature that photographs could help police identify stolen goods. It is one of the first pictures made to record a collection.
Count the cups and jugs. How many different shapes can you find?
The Soliloquy of the Broom
A broom leans in a sunlit doorway. Talbot turned a plain household corner into a picture, showing that photography could find beauty in everyday things.
Why do you think he gave a broom such a grand title?
Bust of Patroclus
Talbot photographed a plaster bust many times in the sun. Statues never moved, so they were perfect first models, and he could show how light changes a face.
Where does the light fall on the face? Where are the deepest shadows?
Dr. Chalmers
Thomas Chalmers was a famous Scottish minister who helped found a new Church of Scotland in 1843. Hill and Adamson took portraits of its founders.
What does his face tell you about him?
Newhaven Fishwives
Hill and Adamson photographed the fishing families of Newhaven, a village near Edinburgh. The women who sold the catch posed in their striped aprons, and the pictures show real working lives.
What jobs do you think these people did every day?
Master Miller
A boy in a tartan kilt stands for a calotype portrait by Hill and Adamson. Children had to be very patient in early photography.
What do you think he was told to do while the camera worked?
Nelson's Column Under Construction
Talbot photographed the great column in Trafalgar Square in London while workers were still building it. It is a rare record of a famous monument before it was finished.
What do you see on the wooden scaffolding?
Lace
A piece of lace is laid out so every thread shows. Talbot included it in his book as a way to show how a camera copies fine details perfectly.
Find a flower pattern in the lace.
The Haystack
A thatched haystack with a ladder leaning on it sits beside a farm. Talbot chose a scene from everyday country life, and the ladder makes you imagine the farmer climbing up.
Where do you think the ladder leads?
Portrait of Mrs. Rigby
A woman in a lace cap and shawl sits beside a table, lit from the side. Hill and Adamson worked in a garden studio in Edinburgh, where sunshine made their exposures shorter.
What details of her clothing can you spot?
Anna Brownell Jameson
Anna Jameson was an Irish-born writer who wrote books about art and about women's lives. Hill and Adamson photographed her in a soft calotype portrait.
What kind of book do you think she is thinking about writing?
A Photograph Through a Microscope
This round daguerreotype was made through a microscope. Within a few years of the invention, scientists were using photographs to record things too small to draw easily.
What do you think is under the microscope?
Henrik Cajander
A Finnish man in a dark coat sits for a daguerreotype in about 1844. Before photography, only wealthy families could afford painted portraits, and now many more people could have their faces saved.
What does his serious look tell you about the time?
A Young Woman in a Daguerreotype
A young woman looks calmly at the camera in this daguerreotype from around 1850. The mirror-bright metal plate makes the picture seem to float.
Imagine she is looking at you. What might she say?
Fern Study
On the left is a dried fern, on the right a blue cyanotype of a fern. John Herschel invented the cyanotype in 1842, and it is the process behind blueprints.
How are the real fern and its blue print alike? How are they different?
Dumbarton Presbytery
Hill and Adamson photographed members of Scottish church councils. Men gather close around a book, which meant they all had to stay still for several seconds.
What do you think they are reading?
